issues.legal_issue: A court hearing a second appeal cannot reverse concurrent findings on a purely factual issue by reappreciating evidence absent an error of law.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court both found that the claimant had not proved that her predecessors were related to the mortgagor and mortgagee’s predecessor.
The High Court recognized that the relationship issue was a question of fact but reappreciated the evidence and reversed those concurrent findings.
The lower courts had considered the documents relied on by the claimant and explained why they did not prove the asserted relationship.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in reappreciating the evidence and reversing the concurrent factual findings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as applicable in the judgment, interference in a second appeal is confined to a question of law. A concurrent finding on a pure question of fact cannot be displaced by reappreciating evidence when the lower courts considered the evidence and committed no error of law.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter is before a court exercising second-appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same finding on a factual issue.
predicates.high_court_reappreciated_evidence: The second-appellate court reconsidered the evidence to reach a different factual finding.

issues.definition: When a second-appellate court reconsiders evidence to depart from a factual finding shared by the courts below, it cannot reverse that finding merely on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed family relationship is not established against opposing parties merely by interested statements in documents when persons able to testify to the relationship do not enter the witness box.
material_facts: The claimant relied on documents in which some predecessors described themselves as descendants of the relevant family members and on a will describing one predecessor as a daughter.
The persons who made or could support those statements were parties to the suit and were available to testify, but did not enter the witness box.
Other defendants denied the relationship, and the available testimony of a family member disputed that some of the alleged heirs were related.
The courts below considered the documents and found that they did not establish the relationship asserted.
issues.conclusion: The documents did not prove the asserted relationship, and the claimant’s predecessors were not proved to be heirs entitled to claim redemption.
issues.legal_principle: Statements by interested persons in documents are not, by themselves, proof of the facts stated when those persons are available but do not submit to cross-examination. A statement in a will that a person is someone’s daughter does not establish a different, unstated relationship. Where opposing parties deny the relationship, it must be proved in a manner that gives them an opportunity to challenge it.

predicates.relationship_disputed: The opposing parties denied the claimed family relationship.
predicates.available_supporting_witnesses_not_testi: Persons available to testify to the claimed relationship did not enter the witness box.
predicates.relationship_claim_resting_on_interested: The claim of relationship depended on statements in documents made by interested persons rather than supporting testimony.

issues.definition: A disputed relationship resting on interested documentary statements is not established when available supporting witnesses do not testify.

issues.legal_issue: A person who openly asserts hostile ownership and remains unchallenged for the applicable period may acquire title by adverse possession, and a later redemption claim cannot defeat that acquired title.
material_facts: A person who was not a mortgagee asserted ownership of the property in an earlier suit and in the pleadings in that suit.
The claimant and her predecessors were aware of that assertion but did not challenge it within the applicable period.
The redemption suit was filed only after that period had elapsed.
issues.conclusion: The non-mortgagee’s title had been perfected by adverse possession before the redemption suit was filed, so relief could not be granted against him or his successors on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: An open and hostile assertion of ownership, left unchallenged for the period required to perfect title by adverse possession, can extinguish the former owner’s ability to recover the property. The Court treated the non-mortgagee’s claim as hostile ownership rather than as a mortgagee’s continuing interest; the ordinary period for a mortgage redemption claim did not preserve a claim against that independently asserted title.

rule.if: redemption_suit and non_mortgagee_hostile_ownership_claim and claimant_aware_of_hostile_claim and no_challenge_within_limitation_window

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking redemption of mortgaged property.
predicates.non_mortgagee_hostile_ownership_claim: A person who was not a mortgagee openly claimed ownership adverse to the former owner.
predicates.claimant_aware_of_hostile_claim: The claimant or the claimant’s predecessors knew of the hostile ownership claim.
predicates.no_challenge_within_limitation_window: The hostile claim was not challenged before the applicable limitation period elapsed.

issues.definition: In a redemption suit, an aware claimant who leaves a non-mortgagee’s hostile ownership claim unchallenged for the applicable limitation period cannot prevent that person’s title from becoming perfected.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to recover property from a transferee for value who received an interest exceeding the mortgagee’s rights is subject to the shorter recovery period running from actual or deemed knowledge, and the claimant must plead and prove that the claim is timely.
material_facts: The suit sought redemption, but the mortgagee or persons claiming as owners made transfers that purported to convey interests exceeding the mortgagee’s rights.
The transferees for value were put in possession, and the transfers or the transferees’ possession were discoverable by the claimant’s predecessors through registration or reasonable inquiry.

The plaint did not allege that the claimant’s predecessors lacked knowledge of the transactions or that the suit was brought within the shorter period after knowledge, and no evidence established timely knowledge.
A later transferee’s redemption of a separate mortgage in his own right did not renew the claimant’s already-barred right against the transfer or give the claimant a fresh right.
The challenged sales were for valuable consideration, and the High Court did not find the relevant sale to be non-bona-fide.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred against the transferees in respect of the transfers that exceeded the mortgagee’s interest; the later redemption did not extend or revive the claimant’s time, and the High Court’s contrary limitation findings could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 134 and 148 of the Limitation Act, 1908, distinguish recovery from a transferee for value who receives an interest exceeding the mortgagee’s rights from redemption against a mortgagee who remains a mortgagee. The shorter period under Article 134 runs from actual or deemed knowledge of the transfer; registration is deemed knowledge, and knowledge may also be attributed where due diligence would have discovered the relevant fact. The plaintiff must plead and prove that the claim is within time. A later redemption by a purchaser claiming independently does not revive the former owner’s time-barred claim. Article 134 requires a transfer for valuable consideration and does not add a separate requirement of bona fides; the Court also stated that the purchaser would receive the protection of Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act in the circumstances considered. Patel Bhudarbhai Maganbhai was distinguished because the transactions there did not establish the same kind of absolute, hostile transfer; the other authorities cited by the claimant were held inapplicable or of no assistance to the facts before the Court.

rule.if: redemption_suit and transfer_for_value and transferee_received_interest_exceeding_mortgage_rights and (actual_knowledge_beyond_limitation_window or deemed_knowledge_beyond_limitation_window) and plaintiff_failed_to_plead_and_prove_timely_claim

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking redemption of mortgaged property.
predicates.transfer_for_value: The property or an interest in it was transferred for valuable consideration.
predicates.transferee_received_interest_exceeding_m: The transfer purported to give the transferee an interest greater than the transferor held as mortgagee.
predicates.actual_knowledge_beyond_limitation_windo: The claimant or the claimant’s predecessors actually knew of the transfer outside the applicable recovery period.
predicates.deemed_knowledge_beyond_limitation_windo: The transfer was registered, or its relevant nature could have been discovered through due diligence, outside the applicable recovery period.
predicates.plaintiff_failed_to_plead_and_prove_time: The plaintiff did not plead and prove that the recovery claim was brought within the applicable period after actual or deemed knowledge.

issues.definition: A recovery claim in a redemption suit is time-barred against a transferee for value who received an interest exceeding the mortgagee’s rights when the claimant had actual or deemed knowledge outside the applicable period and did not plead and prove timely filing.
